headline: High-risk shared-file and MCP pathways: ms-swift can write local artifacts while oh-my-openagent injects runtime MCPs/hooks and broad networked tooling.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: ms-swift reads/writes local files and stdin/stdout, so attacker-controlled content in shared artifacts could be interpreted as instructions. oh-my-openagent uses runtime-injected MCPs and hooks, which increases the chance that untrusted content from ms-swift outputs is treated as actionable. The pair lacks explicit provenance controls, so the pathway exists in common setups.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same workspace or artifact directory
IF oh-my-openagent parses ms-swift-generated text as instructions or tool directives
mitigations: Separate workspaces for the two agents
Disable automatic instruction parsing in downstream prompts
Prefix all exchanged artifacts with a non-executable schema header
Review any shared file before passing it between agents

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents touch files and secrets: ms-swift handles hub_token/sdk-token and writes logs/configuration, while oh-my-openagent touches session history and provider authentication data. Because both have network egress and no isolation is stated between them, shared-workspace leakage is plausible in default operator workflows, though not proven to be automatic.
conditions: IF the same directory contains logs, configs, or session history for both agents
IF either agent uploads or forwards file contents to its backend or external APIs
mitigations: Store secrets in separate directories
Rotate any exposed hub/provider tokens
Disable logging of prompts and file contents
Use distinct OS users or containers
Audit outbound requests for file-content uploads

C_capability_conflict.rationale: ms-swift can write the filesystem and spawn subprocesses, and oh-my-openagent can also spawn subprocesses with full-permissions mode requested plus runtime-injected MCPs/hooks. That creates overlapping write and execution authority over local artifacts and tool state; without stated locking or coordination, concurrent modification conflicts are dangerous by default.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same checkout, cache, or config tree
IF oh-my-openagent runs in full-permissions mode while ms-swift writes outputs there
mitigations: Assign disjoint directories per agent
Run one agent at a time for shared resources
Use file locks around generated artifacts
Disable full-permissions mode unless required
Snapshot and diff shared files before each run

D_cascading_error.rationale: ms-swift can emit training, evaluation, and configuration outputs, and oh-my-openagent exposes team_send_message/team_task_create plus browser and API tooling. If oh-my-openagent treats ms-swift outputs as authoritative, errors can cascade into downstream messages or tasks. The pairwise interaction is inferred rather than directly documented, so uncertainty keeps this at medium.
conditions: IF oh-my-openagent consumes ms-swift-generated outputs without verification
IF those outputs are then used to create tasks, messages, or browser actions
mitigations: Require human review before downstream actions
Add schema validation to exchanged outputs
Mark ms-swift outputs as untrusted by default
Log provenance for every handoff
Use a checksum or signed artifact format

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are open-source and docs-only, but they handle different sensitive classes: ms-swift lists hub_token/sdk-token and training artifacts, while oh-my-openagent handles provider auth prompts and session history. No residency or certification mismatch is documented, so only a limited compliance-gap risk is visible from the profiles.
conditions: IF regulated data is entered into either agent
IF retention or logging settings differ between the two deployments
mitigations: Avoid regulated data in shared runs
Disable prompt/session retention where possible
Document which secrets each agent may store
Separate audit logs by agent
Review vendor data-processing terms before deployment
